Pour cet article, La Converse est allée: For this article, La Converse spoke with citizens from immigrant backgrounds in Montréal and Laval to get their views on the October 5 Quebec election. The people we met were chosen to reflect different experiences of, and relationships to, politics: some follow the campaign closely, others barely or not at all; some will vote, others won’t.
Cette démarche ne vise pas à représenter: This approach is not meant to statistically represent immigrants or to predict how they will vote. Rather, it seeks to show the diversity of concerns, experiences and levels of participation that can lie behind what is sometimes presented as an “immigrant vote.”
<strong>À quelques semaines de l’électio: A few weeks before the October 5 Quebec election, La Converse spoke with citizens from immigrant backgrounds in Montréal and Laval. Some are following the campaign, others barely. Some will vote, others won’t. For some, the election is decided in the grocery basket; for others, in a hospital, a job, a home, or the very definition of their place in Quebec. Their voices speak less of an “immigrant vote” than of a range of relationships to politics.
Au parc Villeray, Henri « Moussa » Bien-: At Parc Villeray, Henri “Moussa” Bien-aimé doesn’t seem particularly concerned about the approaching election. At 33, this construction worker, who arrived from Haiti at age 6, hasn’t voted in years. He voted once, around age 19, with his mother, he recalls. Since then, he has drifted away from the ballot box, as from political news.
Sa mère, confie Moussa, pense que les él: His mother, Moussa confides, thinks elections are more or less decided in advance. He doesn’t go that far, and even acknowledges that voting can help secure “benefits for the people” and improve infrastructure.
Sa vie va bien. « Tant qu’on ne me déran: His life is going well. “As long as nobody bothers me in my neighbourhood,” he sums up, openly acknowledging his disconnection from the country’s political life.<l1> One in three Quebecers did not go to the polls in the 2022 election</l1>, and Moussa is one of them. His relationship to elections is hard to reduce to complete indifference. For him, voting can have consequences, but he doesn’t feel concerned enough to take part.
À Laval, Salim Triaï envisage l’élection: In Laval, Salim Triaï sees the election from an entirely different perspective. At 63, this Algerian who arrived in Quebec 16 years ago votes regularly, as does his partner. That said, Salim hasn’t yet been drawn into the campaign, absorbed, he explains, by his appliance repair business. He will vote nonetheless. Not necessarily because he identifies with a party, but because the act matters. “I vote just to say that I exist,” he says.
Son vote n’est pas un chèque en blanc, a: His vote is not a blank cheque, says the man who was a union executive in a previous life. Avoiding identification with any party, Mr. Triaï has down-to-earth priorities: the price of food, health care, retirement and his children’s future. “When you look at access to care, it’s always the same thing since 2010. […] The wait in the emergency room, you go there, you stay about… – last time, my son stayed 12 hours.”
Au sujet de l’immigration, il se dit peu: On immigration, he says he is not very concerned by the current debates, which he doesn’t follow closely enough. His personal experience of Quebec is rather positive, even excellent, he says, pointing to his daily interactions with customers.
S’il pouvait s’adresser directement aux: If he could speak directly to the party leaders, Salim would first ask them to look beyond Quebec’s borders. “We’re not in an isolated space,” he says. In an interconnected world, “a tremor in the far East, the amplitudes arrive here.” Finally, he would urge them to prepare for the political upheavals that can arise elsewhere. “You’re never safe from a Trump or a Trump 2.0,” he warns.
Ce qui ressort de son témoignage n’est d: What emerges from his account, then, is not a dramatic endorsement or rejection, but a form of minimal, self-aware participation: voting to count, even when you don’t follow everything.
Cette diversité n’est pas anodine. Depui: This diversity is not trivial. Since the early 2000s, Quebec politics has no longer been organized solely around the old sovereignist-federalist divide. The<l1> work of political scientists Éric Bélanger and Jean-François Godbout</l1> shows the emergence of another important axis, centred on the management of ethnocultural diversity. In the 2022 election, this identity-based divide helped distinguish the parties’ electorates. But in everyday life, these major fault lines take less theoretical forms.
David Tran, lui, ne suivait pas réelleme: David Tran, for his part, didn’t really follow politics until recently. At Parc Villeray, this Montréal native, who has lived in the neighbourhood for about twenty years, is enjoying the nice weather with his partner and their baby on this September day.
Enseignant en informatique, David a long: A computer science teacher, David long ignored voting, but this time, he says, he doesn’t want to miss the appointment. The reason? Immigration is now an issue directly tied to his job. At the institution where he teaches, a good part of the student body is made up of international students. But the drop in that clientele over the past two years means, according to him, fewer cohorts, and could therefore mean fewer contracts for him. “We’re a bit short of students. Before, most of the customers were international students. So now, there are fewer customers. And if there are fewer customers, no group opens. […] And no group opening means no contract for the teachers,” he fears.
Ce qui pourrait apparaître, dans le déba: What might look, in public debate, like a statistic about immigration thresholds thus becomes a very concrete question: will I still have work?
David dit se sentir parfaitement Québéco: David says he feels perfectly Québécois, but adds that immigration policies now have a measurable impact on his career. For him, the cost of living remains the other major concern.
S’il pouvait s’adresser aux chefs de par: If he could speak to the party leaders, he would ask them to review immigration policy, but also to pay more attention to the cost of living. “If you look at inflation, it has really gone up in the past five, six years, during COVID. So I don’t know if in a few years we’ll still be able to afford groceries like before,” he says.
À Cartierville, Midelene Lubins regarde: In Cartierville, Midelene Lubins looks at politics from yet another position. Having arrived from Haiti with her family, this woman in her forties is now a single mother of five children, all born in Quebec.
Chez elle, la politique commence à l’épi: For her, politics starts at the grocery store. “Life has become expensive,” she says. Housing weighs on her budget, even in public housing (HLM), since her contribution rises with her income. Then there is food, which is especially expensive with five children, including teenagers. She estimates that a “good basket” of groceries, which used to cost her $200 to $300, now costs her about $700.
Sur cette question, l’expérience de Mide: On this point, the experience of Midelene, Salim and the others fits into a broader trend: according to the<l1> 2026 Canada’s Food Price Report</l1>, food prices in Canada are 27% higher today than five years ago. And despite slowing inflation, the report still forecasts a 4 to 6% increase in food prices in 2026, including in Quebec. For a family of four, the researchers estimate that the annual grocery bill will reach nearly $17,600, about $1,000 more than in 2025.
La santé est l’autre grande préoccupatio: Health is Midelene’s other major concern. She laments how hard it is to see a doctor quickly when a child is sick and says she sometimes feels she has to make endless calls and visits before finding a spot. Safety also matters to her. When she talks about racial profiling, her thoughts quickly turn to her 19-year-old son, whom she worries about every time he goes out with his friends.
Son travail de préposée aux bénéficiaire: Her work as a patient attendant in a health centre also gives her a particular point of view on the transformations of the health care system, notably the reduction of attendant teams, which, she says, is increasing workloads. It is also a deciding factor in her choice, because, Midelene says, her vote will go to the party that intends to abolish Santé Québec and return to the CIUSSS, an organization she considered more efficient.
Malgré tout cela, Midelene ira voter, mê: Despite all this, Midelene will go vote, even though she doesn’t put much faith in politicians’ promises. Asked whether they understand the reality of a single mother working to support five children, her answer is curt: “I don’t think so. They already have their gold or silver spoon in their mouth.”
Amine Benkara arrive dans cette mosaïque: Amine Benkara enters this mosaic with a much more intense relationship to politics. At 37, this immigrant who arrived in Quebec in 2022 under the Regular Skilled Worker Program has just obtained his Canadian citizenship. The provincial election will be his first chance to vote as a citizen. And he fully intends to use it. “I actually believe in one thing: that your voice won’t be stolen,” he says.
Amine suit les débats, consulte les prog: Amine follows the debates, reads the platforms, watches political shows, and above all, he faces the reality of housing, the cost of living, wages, taxes and public services. His experience has led him, however, to temper the idealized image of a Quebec where “everything is beautiful, everything is fine, everything is above board.”
Il dénonce notamment ce qu’il considère: He denounces in particular what he considers a waste of public money and projects that drag on, citing, among others, SAAQclic and the difficulties with social housing. But what concerns him most goes beyond questions of governance. As a young worker and future homeowner, he thinks about housing, the cost of living, wages and taxes. If he had the party leaders in front of him, he would ask them a very concrete question: “What are you going to do for the next five years?” Not just promises, he insists, but “a very specific, very clear plan” to improve the situation of the middle class.
L’immigration demeure néanmoins une dime: Immigration nevertheless remains an important dimension of his choice. Amine believes that some political rhetoric targeting minorities has hardened in recent years. He says he identifies more with some of Québec solidaire’s proposals, notably on housing, lowering the cost of living and redistributing wealth.
Mais au-delà des programmes, Amine aimer: But beyond platforms, Amine would like politicians to get closer to the daily reality of immigrant workers, by inviting them to take the bus at the end of the day. “They would really see the people who work hard for this country,” he says. It is also this population that he would like to see given more consideration in political debates.
Marianna Gutierrez Herrera, 25 ans, se s: Marianna Gutierrez Herrera, 25, stands at the other end of the spectrum. She arrived from Colombia with her parents in 2004 and is now a graduate student in political science at Université de Montréal, working with humanitarian organizations alongside immigrants. Her interest in politics thus comes not only from books or university courses, but is also fed by what she sees on the ground.
Pour Marianna, l’immigration est le prin: For Marianna, immigration is the main issue of this election. Next come safety, police violence, education and health. She wants debates on safety, in particular, to take greater account of what happens in neighbourhoods with large racialized populations. But she doesn’t feel represented by the political class. “Representation doesn’t always equal concrete answers or concrete change,” she says.
Cette distinction entre présence et repr: This distinction between presence and representation echoes the findings of a<l1> study</l1> on political representation in Quebec by Benjamin Ferland and Éric Desrochers. The researchers paint a complex picture: some groups, notably women and less-educated people, appear less well represented on certain dimensions, but no group is systematically so. Young people are even sometimes better represented than the other groups studied.
Chez Marianna, cette question devient pe: For Marianna, this question becomes personal. As a young racialized woman, she says she sees few women of colour in places of power and sometimes feels pressure not to “make waves.”
Elle vit pourtant elle-même certaines de: Yet she herself experiences some of the difficulties that dominate the campaign, notably around housing. Marianna still lives with her parents and makes long daily commutes to Université de Montréal because she can’t afford to rent on the island. But even so, she refuses to reduce her political choice to her personal comfort.
Six personnes, six rapports aux élection: Six people, six relationships to elections. One doesn’t vote; another votes to feel that he exists; a mother of five looks at promises through the price of her grocery basket and working conditions in the health care system; a teacher discovers that immigration policy can decide, indirectly, his next contract; a new citizen sees in his first vote a way to take part in Quebec’s future; a young political scientist seeks to understand why public policy responds so poorly to the realities she observes.
Difficile, dans ces conditions, de parle: It’s hard, under these conditions, to speak of an “immigrant vote.” Research by political scientists Éric Bélanger and Jean-François Godbout on Quebecers’ voting behaviour shows, moreover, that the system has become more fragmented. The old face-off between sovereignism and federalism no longer suffices to explain electoral choices: economic divides and those tied to ethnocultural diversity now occupy an important place.
Sur le terrain, cette fragmentation ne r: On the ground, this fragmentation doesn’t necessarily look like an ideological debate. These voices therefore don’t tell us how “immigrants” will vote, but instead show something simpler and harder to measure: the same ballots can carry radically different expectations.
